overview.description: Two-player plain-trick game: 13 cards each, trump from the turned card on the stock. First 13 tricks are played with the winner taking the face-up stock card and the loser the face-down one; then 13 tricks without replenishment. The player who wins the majority of the second-stage tricks wins the hand.

history.origins: Two-player Whist variant of British origin; also known as German Whist and Chinese whist.
timeline: 1894: Rules recorded in London periodical Home Notes; 1897: appears in Foster's Encyclopedia of Games in America.

nullReasons.evolution: No documented evolutionary changes; game emerged as a stable tradition.
nullReasons.cultural: No specific cultural or regional significance documented beyond its origins.

setup.players: Two players only, using a standard 52-card pack. The players agree who deals first (often by cutting the pack); the turn to deal alternates after each hand. The dealer offers the pack to the non-dealer for cutting before dealing.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Rank A (high) K Q J 10 9 8 7 6 5 4 3 2 (low) in each suit.
setup.dealing: Dealer gives 13 cards to each player, one at a time. The 27th card is placed face-up on top of the remaining stock; its suit is trump for the hand.

rules.objective: Win the majority of the 13 tricks in the second stage of play, after the stock is exhausted.
rules.gameplay: Non-dealer leads to the first trick. Each trick: leader plays any card; second player must follow suit if able, otherwise may play any card. Same suit: higher card wins. Different suits: leader wins unless second plays a trump, then trump wins. Winner of a trick takes the face-up card from the stock into hand; loser takes the next face-down card. Winner leads to the next trick. After 13 tricks the stock is empty; then 13 more tricks are played without replenishment. Majority of those final 13 tricks wins the hand.
keyRules: Winner of trick takes face-up stock card, loser takes face-down.

strategy.basic: In the first 13 tricks, try to win only when the face-up stock card is better than the hidden one. Save high cards and trumps for the second stage when tricks count.

nullReasons.intermediate: No distinct intermediate tier; strategy scales with memory and stock play.
nullReasons.advanced: Advanced play is full two-player Whist strategy; no separate advanced tier.

nullReasons.medium: No distinct medium tier; all non-easy AI uses stock and trick strategy.
